templates.title: Cache hit ratio per zone and content type, under a stated counting rule
templates.subtopic: classification before aggregation, conditional counts, HAVING floors, longest-match joins

sections.scenario: A customer's dashboard shows how much of their traffic the edge cache served, per zone (a domain the customer has added) and per content type. Customers compare it across zones and argue with it, so the counting rule is written down: a response served from cache counts as a hit even if the edge first revalidated it with the origin, and requests the cache could never have served (bypassed by a rule, or uncacheable by nature) are not part of the ratio at all. A ratio over a handful of requests means nothing, so small groups are hidden. You have one day of request logs ({{requests}} rows) and the list of {{zone_count}} zones.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns zone_name, content_type, cacheable_requests, cache_hits, hit_ratio, ordered by zone_name, content_type. Each request belongs to the zone whose zone_name equals its host or is a suffix of it after a dot (img.example.com is in example.com). Under this exercise's rule, cache_status hit and revalidated are hits; miss and expired are misses; bypass and dynamic are excluded. cacheable_requests counts hits plus misses, cache_hits the hits, and hit_ratio is ROUND(cache_hits / cacheable_requests, 4). Report a (zone, content type) group only if it has at least {{min_cacheable}} cacheable requests. {{status_rule}} {{ct_rule}} {{zone_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The floor is inclusive and counts cacheable requests only. Use the exact zone-matching rule above: a plain "ends with" test is not enough.
sections.assumptions: The statuses, their classification and the floor are this exercise's rules; real products define their cache statuses and analytics in their own documentation, so check current docs. Traffic, hosts and zones are hypothetical; example.* names are placeholders.
sections.criteria: Classifies statuses exactly as stated (revalidated, and stale and updating where present, as hits; bypass and dynamic excluded); a floor on cacheable requests, inclusive; content types normalised (Hard+); a dot-respecting zone match with the longest zone winning and unmatched hosts dropped (Very Hard); correct rounding; deterministic order; can discuss byte weighting, sampling and rollups.

clarifications.q: Why is a revalidated response a hit?
clarifications.a: Under this exercise's rule the body came from the cache; the edge only asked the origin whether it was still fresh. The origin did not send it again.

clarifications.q: Do bypassed requests count as misses?
clarifications.a: No. They are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator.

clarifications.q: Is the floor applied to all requests or to cacheable ones?
clarifications.a: Cacheable ones. A group with many bypassed requests but few cacheable ones is hidden.

clarifications.q: Is www.example.com in zone example.com?
clarifications.a: Yes: the zone name follows a dot. example.com itself is also in it.

clarifications.q: What do I return for a group below the floor?
clarifications.a: Nothing: leave the row out.

hints: Classify first: one row per request with its zone, its normalised content type and a hit flag, with excluded statuses filtered out.
Match zones with host = zone_name OR right(host, length(zone_name) + 1) = '.' || zone_name; if several zones match, keep the longest with ROW_NUMBER() or DISTINCT ON.
Then COUNT(*), COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE is_hit) and a HAVING COUNT(*) >= … on the classified rows.
followups: Product wants the same ratio weighted by bytes instead of requests. How does the query change, and why can the two ratios disagree sharply for one zone?
The logs reaching you are sampled, and each line carries how many requests it stands for. What changes, and what happens to the floor?
At billions of requests a day, would you compute this from raw logs on every dashboard load? Describe the rollup you would keep and its grain.
A customer says the ratio dropped overnight with no change on their side. Which questions about the counting rule and the data would you ask before looking at the cache itself?

rules.ask: Is the ratio the average of per-request flags, the average of per-hour ratios, or the ratio of the totals? Which one does the dashboard need, and does it matter here?
Does your suffix test put cdn.myexample.net in zone example.net? How do you make it respect the dot?
Your HAVING counts which rows: all requests, or only cacheable ones? What does a group with many bypassed requests do to it?
Which normalisation do you apply first, and what does Text/HTML ; charset=utf-8 become in your query?
If each line stands for several requests, do you apply the floor to lines or to the weighted count, and why?

templates.title: Origin 5xx share per zone and hour, with edge-generated errors kept apart
templates.subtopic: outer joins, latest row per key, hourly buckets, ratio floors

sections.scenario: When a visitor sees an error, the customer needs to know whose problem it is. Some errors come from the customer's own origin server: the edge forwarded the request and the origin answered 5xx. Others are generated at the edge because no answer came back at all, and those belong in a separate column. A support engineer wants, per zone and hour, the share of forwarded requests the origin failed, so a customer can see when their origin was in trouble. You have the request log ({{requests}} requests) and one row per origin attempt that received an HTTP response ({{attempts}} attempts).
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns zone_name, hour_start, forwarded, origin_5xx, origin_5xx_share, edge_errors, ordered by zone_name, hour_start, where hour_start is request_ts truncated to the UTC hour. A request is forwarded if it has at least one row in origin_attempts. A forwarded request is an origin error if its outcome origin_status is between 500 and 599. A request with no attempts and edge_status 500 or above is an edge-generated error: it is counted in edge_errors only, never in forwarded. origin_5xx_share is ROUND(origin_5xx / forwarded, 4). Report a zone-hour only if it has at least {{min_forwarded}} forwarded requests. {{edge_rule}} {{attempt_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). 4xx statuses are not errors for this report. Requests served from cache, or blocked at the edge with a 4xx, have no attempts and are neither forwarded nor errors.
sections.assumptions: The classification is this exercise's rule; which edge error codes a real product uses, and when, is described in its own documentation, so check current docs. Statuses, zones and volumes are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Separates forwarded requests (with an attempt) from edge-generated errors (no attempt, 5xx at the edge); judges origin errors by origin_status, not the status the visitor saw (Hard+); one outcome per request from its last attempt (Very Hard); 4xx excluded; floor on forwarded requests, inclusive; UTC hours; correct rounding; can discuss local time, finer grains and alert thresholds.

clarifications.q: An origin returned 503 but the visitor got a 200 from a stale cached copy. Is it an origin error?
clarifications.a: Yes. The report is about the origin, so judge origin_status.

clarifications.q: Does an edge-generated error count toward the floor?
clarifications.a: No. The floor counts forwarded requests only.

clarifications.q: Which hour is 03:59:59.999 in?
clarifications.a: 03:00. Truncate, do not round.

clarifications.q: Are zone-hours with no forwarded requests reported?
clarifications.a: No; they are below any floor.

clarifications.q: Is a 404 from the origin an error here?
clarifications.a: No. Only 5xx.

hints: Reduce origin_attempts to one outcome per request first; DISTINCT ON (request_id) … ORDER BY request_id, attempt_no DESC is one way.
LEFT JOIN the outcome onto every request: a NULL outcome means not forwarded, and that is where edge errors live.
One classified row per request (forwarded, origin_5xx, edge_error flags), then COUNT(*) FILTER (…) per zone and date_trunc('hour', request_ts).
followups: The customer's dashboard is in their own time zone. Which hours move, and what happens on a day the clocks change?
Their origin sits behind several data centres; the support engineer wants the share per origin address. What do you need in the log, and how does the floor interact with the finer grain?
The same query over a month of logs for a large zone is slow. What would you precompute every hour, and can you still apply the floor afterwards?
An alert fires when the share exceeds 5% for two hours running. What false alarms does a low-traffic zone produce, and how would you design the threshold to avoid them?

rules.ask: With an inner join, where do the requests with no attempts go, and how do you still count the edge-generated errors?
A stale copy hides an origin 503 behind a 200. Which column does your error test read?
The edge retried and the second attempt returned 200. Is that request an origin error in your query?
Are you counting requests or attempts in the denominator? What does a request with three attempts contribute?
In which time zone does your date_trunc run, and what makes that explicit rather than a session default?

templates.title: DNS records that flapped — real changes per record and UTC day
templates.subtopic: LAG over change history, null-safe comparison, per-day counts, value normalisation

sections.scenario: Customers manage DNS records for their zones through a dashboard, an API and automation such as failover scripts. A record whose answer keeps changing back and forth usually means two automations are fighting, and resolvers around the world see a moving target. A reliability team wants a daily list of records that flapped. The change log is noisy: automation often rewrites a record with the value it already had, which changes nothing a resolver sees. You have the change log for a few days ({{changes}} rows).
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns zone_name, record_name, record_type, change_date, changes: for each record and UTC date of changed_at, the number of real changes, keeping only rows where changes is greater than {{k}}. Order by zone_name, change_date, record_name, record_type. Order a record's rows by changed_at, then change_id. A row is a real change when its value differs from the record's previous row's value, wherever that previous row falls (it may be on an earlier day). A record's first row is its creation and is never a change. {{identity_rule}} {{value_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). "More than {{k}}" is strict. The previous row is the record's previous row in the whole log, not within the day.
sections.assumptions: The flapping rule and the threshold are this exercise's; real DNS products keep audit logs with their own schemas and semantics, so check current docs. Zones, names and addresses are hypothetical, using documentation address ranges.
sections.criteria: LAG across days within the record, ordered with change_id as the tie-break; same-value rewrites ignored; creation row excluded; strict threshold; record identity includes the type (Hard+); deletions and re-creations counted with null-safe comparison and values normalised (Very Hard); deterministic order; can discuss actors, record sets, TTLs and incremental computation.

clarifications.q: The record was set to the value it already had. Is that a change?
clarifications.a: No. Nothing a resolver sees changed.

clarifications.q: The first change on Tuesday restores the value from Monday morning. Is it a change?
clarifications.a: Compare it with the previous row, which is Monday's last value. If that differs, yes.

clarifications.q: Is creating a record a change?
clarifications.a: No. The first row of a record is its creation.

clarifications.q: Exactly {{k}} changes in a day: reported?
clarifications.a: No. More than {{k}}.

clarifications.q: Two rows share a timestamp.
clarifications.a: Order them by change_id.

hints: LAG(new_value) OVER (PARTITION BY <record> ORDER BY changed_at, change_id) gives the previous value across days.
Use IS DISTINCT FROM rather than <> if a value can be NULL; <> with a NULL is neither true nor false.
Keep ROW_NUMBER() from the same window to drop the creation row, then group by record and (changed_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date.
followups: The team wants to know which actor (dashboard user, API token, automation) caused each flap. What would you add to the log, and how would you report "two actors alternating"?
A record with several values (a set of A records for one name) is changed by adding and removing members. How would you define a "real change" for a set?
Flapping matters only if resolvers saw it. How would you relate the change log to the record's TTL to estimate how many changes could actually have been observed?
The log covers millions of zones. How would you partition and incrementally compute this report each day without rescanning history, given that the previous value can be months old?

rules.ask: The first change of a day compares with what? What does a window partitioned by date do to it?
What does new_value <> prev_value return when one side is NULL, and which rows does that drop?
A record went A → B → A → B. How many distinct values is that, and how many changes?
What is in your LAG's PARTITION BY? Is the record type part of the record's identity?
Which values does that normalisation affect, and could it ever merge two answers that really differ?

templates.title: Resolving a bulk redirect list — final target, hops and loops
templates.subtopic: functional graphs, memoised iterative walks, cycle detection

sections.scenario: A customer migrating a large site uploads a bulk redirect list: tens of thousands of rules, each sending one URL to another with a status code. Over years of migrations the list has grown chains (old → older → current) and, now and then, loops that send visitors round in circles. Before the list goes live, a validator reports for every source where a visitor would finally land, how many redirects it would take, and whether every hop on the way is permanent, which matters to search engines and caches.
sections.problem: Implement resolve_redirects(rules). rules is a list of (source_url, target_url, status_code); URLs are written host/path. Following a URL means: if it is a source, go to its target (one hop); stop at the first URL that is not a source. Return a dict with one entry per distinct source: (final_url, hops, permanent), where permanent is True only if every hop on the chain has status 301 or 308. If following a source ever revisits a URL, the chain never ends: return (None, -1, False) for it. {{dup_rule}} {{canon_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to about 150 000 rules, with chains thousands of hops long. Following each source's chain from scratch is quadratic on such lists; aim for O(number of rules). CPython's default recursion limit is about 1 000.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical sites and rules. The matching and canonicalisation rules are this exercise's; real redirect features have their own options (for example subpath matching or query-string handling), so check current docs. 302 and 307 are temporary, 301 and 308 permanent.
sections.criteria: Correct final URL, hop count and permanence along each chain; loops, including chains that lead into them, returned as the sentinel; first rule wins for repeated sources and self-redirects are loops (Hard+); canonical forms applied to sources and targets, keeping the root slash and path case (Very Hard); one memoised iterative pass, O(n); a clear complexity argument; credible discussion of flattening, subpath rules and incremental validation.

clarifications.q: Is a target that is not a source the final URL even on another host?
clarifications.a: Yes. Any URL that is not a source ends the chain.

clarifications.q: A source leads into a loop it is not part of.
clarifications.a: It never ends either: (None, -1, False).

clarifications.q: Does a single 302 anywhere on the chain make it non-permanent?
clarifications.a: Yes, for every source whose chain passes through it.

clarifications.q: Do I return entries for targets that are not sources?
clarifications.a: No. Only for sources.

clarifications.q: Can I recurse?
clarifications.a: Chains are thousands of hops long; an iterative walk is safer.

hints: Build next[source] = (target, is_permanent) first; every later step is a lookup.
A source's answer is its target's answer plus one hop. Walk forward collecting unresolved URLs on a list, then fill them in backwards.
Track which URLs are on the current walk: meeting one again means a cycle, and every URL on that walk, including the lead-in, gets the loop result.
followups: The validator must also suggest a fix: rewrite each rule to point straight at its final URL. Which rules change, and what must you not rewrite?

Rules can match a source and all its subpaths, appending the rest of the path to the target. Why does that make "follow until not a source" possibly endless without a loop, and what limit would you add?
The list is edited one rule at a time in a UI and validated after every edit. How would you update the answers incrementally instead of recomputing everything?
How would you report loops to a customer so they can fix them quickly: which URLs would you show, and in what order?

rules.ask: The test chains are 3 000 hops long. What does your recursion do at depth 1 000, and how do you make it iterative?
Is your visited set per walk or global? What goes wrong if a URL resolved in an earlier walk is treated as "on the current path"?
How many steps does following every chain from scratch take for 40 chains of 3 000 hops?
How do you memoise a URL whose chain is still being walked, and how do you tell that apart from a cycle?
Do you canonicalise the targets as well as the sources, and what happens to a rule whose target is just another spelling of its source?

templates.title: Was the cached copy purged before this request?
templates.subtopic: per-key sorted timelines, interval existence queries, path prefixes

sections.scenario: Customers label cached responses with cache tags (product-42, homepage) and, when content changes, purge by tag rather than URL by URL. A support team investigating "visitors saw the old price" replays the logs: for each request served from a cached copy, was that copy already invalidated by a purge, so the visitor should have received a fresh one? The replay has to run over a day of a busy zone's requests and purges.
sections.problem: Implement invalidated(purges, requests). purges is a list of (purge_ts, zone, kind, value); kind is 'tag' (value is a tag), 'everything' (value None) or 'prefix' (value is a path prefix). requests is a list of (request_ts, zone, path, cached_at, tags): the copy that served the request was stored at cached_at and carries tags; cached_at <= request_ts. Return a list of booleans, one per request in order: True if some purge in the same zone that matches the copy has cached_at <= purge_ts <= request_ts. A tag purge matches when its tag is one of the copy's tags (exact, case-sensitive). {{zone_rule}} {{prefix_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 100 000 requests and 60 000 purges; a tag can be purged thousands of times. Checking every purge for every request is far too slow, and so is scanning all of one tag's purges per request. Times are integer seconds.
sections.assumptions: The purge kinds, matching rules and inclusive boundaries are this exercise's; real purge features differ in what they support and how quickly a purge takes effect, so check current docs. Here a purge takes effect at its own timestamp everywhere. Zones, paths and tags are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Inclusive boundaries on both ends; exact tag matching; zone isolation and purge-everything (Hard+); prefix purges on whole path segments, including a prefix equal to the path (Very Hard); per-key sorted times with binary search rather than scans; a clear complexity argument (O((p + q·k) log p)); credible discussion of first-purge attribution, per-location propagation and batch replay.

clarifications.q: A purge happened at exactly cached_at.
clarifications.a: The copy counts as invalidated: both boundaries are inclusive.

clarifications.q: A purge happened at exactly request_ts.
clarifications.a: Also invalidated.

clarifications.q: Does a purge of product touch a copy tagged product-42?
clarifications.a: No. Tags match exactly.

clarifications.q: A purge happened before the copy was stored.
clarifications.a: It cannot affect that copy: the copy was stored afterwards.

clarifications.q: What if the copy has no tags?
clarifications.a: Tag purges never match it.

hints: The question per (request, key) is "is there a purge time in [cached_at, request_ts]?". Group purge times by (zone, kind, value) and sort each list once.
bisect_left(times, cached_at) finds the first purge at or after caching; the copy is invalidated if that time exists and is at or before request_ts.
A request checks only the keys that could match it: its zone's purge-everything, each of its tags, and (if prefixes exist) each whole-segment prefix of its path.
followups: Support now wants, for each invalidated request, which purge invalidated it first. What changes in the lookup?
Purges do not take effect everywhere at the same instant; each location reports when it applied the purge. How would you redo the replay per location?
The replay must cover a month for a zone with a billion requests. How would you run it as a batch job, and what would you join on?
A customer purges by tag thousands of times an hour from a deploy script. What would you show them about the cost of that, using only these logs?

rules.ask: How many purge comparisons does your loop make for 100 000 requests against 60 000 purges?
Which side do you bisect on, and how does your comparison keep both boundaries inclusive?
Does your prefix check treat /img as covering /images/hero.jpg? How do you stop it at a segment boundary?
What is the key of your index? Where does the zone go, and what happens if two zones use the same tag?
You sort once per key. What is the total cost, and what if purges arrive as a stream while requests are being replayed?

templates.title: Weighted hashing ring for an origin pool — where each key goes, and what moves
templates.subtopic: consistent hashing with weighted virtual nodes, sorted ring and binary search

sections.scenario: A customer's site sits behind an edge network, and its traffic is served by a pool of origin servers. To keep each origin's cache warm, every request key (here, the URL path) should keep going to the same origin, and when one origin is taken out for maintenance only the keys it was serving should move. Origins differ in size, so a bigger origin should get a proportionally bigger share. A hashing ring with weighted virtual points does all three. In this exercise you write the routine that builds the ring and routes keys; the hashing rule is this exercise's rule, not a description of any product's load balancer (check current docs for real steering options).
sections.problem: Implement route_keys(origins, keys, vnodes, remove=None, detail=False). origins is a list of (name, weight) with distinct names and integer weights ≥ 0. Origin name places weight * vnodes points on the ring: point i (for i from 0 to weight * vnodes − 1) sits at position ring_hash(name + "#" + str(i)), using the ring_hash function given in the starter code, unchanged. Order all points by (position, origin name, i). A key belongs to the first point in that order whose position is greater than or equal to ring_hash(key). If no point qualifies, it wraps round to the first point of all. Return the list of origin names, one per entry of keys, in the same order. If the pool has no points at all (no origins, or every weight is 0), return None. {{remove_rule}} {{detail_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 60 origins, weights up to 5, vnodes up to 200, and 100 000 keys. Keys are ASCII strings and may repeat. Something close to O(V log V + n log V) for V points and n keys is expected. Scanning every point for every key is too slow at these sizes.
sections.assumptions: The pool, weights and traffic are hypothetical. Origins are always healthy in this exercise, so routing depends only on the ring. Two different points can, rarely, share a position; the ordering rule above decides between them.
sections.criteria: Exactly the given hash and point naming; points ordered by position, then origin name, then index; inclusive comparison and wrap-around; None for a pool without points; weight 0 handled as no points; repeated keys reported and counted for each entry; a sorted ring with binary search rather than a scan per key; for removal, the observation that only the removed origin's keys can move; a clear complexity argument; credible answers on virtual-node spread, churn and hot keys.

clarifications.q: Is the comparison with the key's hash inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. A point whose position equals the key's hash owns the key.

clarifications.q: What happens to a key whose hash is larger than every point?
clarifications.a: It wraps round to the first point in the ring's order.

clarifications.q: Can I use Python's built-in hash() or hashlib?
clarifications.a: No. Use the starter's ring_hash exactly, so that every answer is reproducible.

clarifications.q: Does a weight of 0 mean the origin is in the pool?
clarifications.a: It is listed but owns no points, so it never receives a key. That is how a drained origin looks.

clarifications.q: Do the origins arrive in any particular order?
clarifications.a: No. The answer depends only on the points, not on the order of origins.

hints: Build the list of points once, sort it, and keep the positions in a separate list. One binary search per key then finds the first position at or after the key's hash.
bisect_left on the sorted positions returns the first index whose position is greater than or equal to the hash. An index equal to the length means wrap to 0.
Removing an origin does not change any other origin's points. Which keys can possibly change origin, and where can they go?
followups: Why give each origin many virtual points rather than one? What happens to the spread of keys with vnodes = 1, and how would you measure the imbalance?
Origins need to be added and removed several times a minute. What would you change so that you do not rebuild and re-sort the whole ring each time?
An origin is unhealthy for 30 seconds. Removing it moves its keys; is that what you want for such a short outage, and what would you do instead?
A single key (one very popular asset) is more traffic than one origin can serve. How would you change the scheme without losing cache affinity for every other key?

rules.ask: The starter gives you a hash. Why does it matter that every process in the edge network computes exactly the same hash for a key, and what does Python's built-in hash do across processes?
With hash(key) % number_of_origins, what fraction of keys move when one origin of twenty is removed? Compare that with your ring.
Your search returns an index equal to the length of the list. What does that mean for the key, and which test catches it?
How much work is a full rebuild for each pool change at 60 origins and 200 points per unit of weight, and how often can you afford it?
An origin's weight goes from 2 to 3. Which keys move, and in which direction?

templates.title: Peak requests per second over many dashboard ranges
templates.subtopic: sparse table for range maximum, clipping, tie-breaking

sections.scenario: An analytics dashboard for one zone (a customer's domain on the edge network) shows requests per second over the last few days. Customers drag over the chart to select a time range, and the dashboard shows the peak requests per second inside it. A page with many panels, comparisons and alert previews asks for tens of thousands of ranges over the same series, so each range must be answered without rescanning it.
sections.problem: Implement range_peaks(samples, ranges, with_time=False). samples is a list of (second, requests) rows for one zone, where second is a Unix epoch second and requests a non-negative integer. The series covers every second from the earliest to the latest second in samples. {{rows_rule}} ranges is a list of (first, last) pairs, both inclusive epoch seconds. Clip each range to the series. If no second remains, or first > last, the answer for that range is None. Otherwise it is the largest requests count of any second in the clipped range. {{time_rule}} Return one answer per range, in order. If samples is empty, every answer is None.
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 seconds and 200 000 ranges. Ranges can be as long as the series. Something close to O(n log n + q) or O(n + q log n) is expected. Scanning each range is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Traffic numbers are hypothetical. Requests per second are exact counts in this exercise (no sampling). Seconds are UTC epoch seconds, so there are no time-zone or daylight-saving gaps.
sections.criteria: Inclusive ranges clipped to the series; None for ranges with nothing left and for an empty series; correct peak and, where asked, the earliest second on ties; for unsorted rows, seconds summed and missing seconds treated as 0; a sparse table (or another structure with a sound bound) built once and used for every range; correct overlap of the two halves; a clear complexity argument; sensible answers on streaming updates, resolutions and many zones.

clarifications.q: Are both ends of a range included?
clarifications.a: Yes. (t, t) is a one-second range.

clarifications.q: What if a range starts before the first sample?
clarifications.a: Clip it to the series. Only a range with nothing left after clipping is None.

clarifications.q: Can the same range be asked twice?
clarifications.a: Yes. Answer it each time.

clarifications.q: May I sort or preprocess the samples?
clarifications.a: Yes. Preprocessing once is the point; the ranges are the many queries.

clarifications.q: Are the values small?
clarifications.a: They fit comfortably in a Python int. Do not assume a small maximum.

hints: The maximum of a range is the maximum of two overlapping ranges that together cover it. Overlap does not matter for a maximum, as it would for a sum.
Precompute, for every start and every power of two 2^k, the maximum of the 2^k seconds from that start. Each level is built from the one below in linear time.
To keep the earliest second on ties, store something whose maximum prefers a larger value and then a smaller second, for example a tuple (value, -second) or one integer that encodes both.
followups: New seconds arrive every second while the dashboard is open. Which structure would you use so that appending is cheap and ranges stay fast?
The dashboard also shows the total requests in the range. What would you precompute for that, and why is it simpler than the maximum?
The series is stored at one-second resolution for a day, one-minute for a month and one-hour for a year. Which resolution answers a 10-day range, and what does the peak mean then?
The same peaks are needed for 50 000 zones on a shared analytics cluster. Where do you compute them, and what do you keep in memory?

rules.ask: A segment tree answers in O(log n) and supports updates. What does it cost per range here, and when would you prefer it to a sparse table?
How many seconds does max(series[a:b]) read over 100 000 ranges of a two-day series, and how long would that take?
A running maximum from the start answers ranges that start at the first second. What breaks for a range that starts in the middle?
How does your stored value make the maximum prefer the earlier second on a tie? Show it on two equal peaks.
With blocks of √n seconds, how much work is one range, and is that fast enough at 200 000 ranges?

templates.title: Debug the zone analytics rollup
templates.subtopic: sampling weights, retried delivery, nanosecond time, IPv6 prefixes

sections.scenario: An analytics pipeline turns edge request log lines into an hourly rollup per zone: requests, bytes served, bytes served from cache, and how many distinct client networks were seen. High-volume zones are sampled, so a log line can stand for many requests. Customers have raised several complaints. Some hours show more bytes served from cache than bytes served in total. Requests near the end of an hour appear in the next hour. Request counts jump after a log delivery is retried. A cache ratio by bytes looks worse than the customer's own measurements. Zones with many IPv6 visitors report far more distinct client networks than expected. The rollup below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix zone_rollup(lines) so that it meets this specification. {{replay_rule}} Each line is a dict {"zone", "ray", "batch", "ts_ns", "sample_interval", "bytes", "cache_status", "client_ip"}.

  1. One request, one line. ray identifies a request uniquely across all zones. A retried delivery can repeat a line in a later batch. Count each ray once and ignore later copies.
  2. Hour. ts_ns is an integer number of nanoseconds since the Unix epoch, UTC. The line's hour is the epoch second at the start of its UTC hour.
  3. Sampling. A line with sample_interval = k stands for k requests, each with the line's bytes. Requests and both byte totals are weighted by k.
  4. Cached bytes. In this exercise's rule, responses with cache_status hit, revalidated or updating were served from cache; every other status was not (check current docs for real cache statuses).
  5. Client networks. An IPv4 client is its own network. An IPv6 client's network is its /64 prefix, whatever way the address is written. The count is of distinct networks among the counted lines and is not weighted.
  6. Output. A list of [zone, hour, requests, bytes, cached_bytes, networks], one per zone and hour that has lines, sorted by zone and then hour.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 lines, processed in linear time. The standard library (including ipaddress) is available.
sections.assumptions: Log fields, statuses and the sampling scheme are hypothetical and simplified, not a product's log format. IPv6 addresses are in hexadecimal notation, possibly compressed with :: and in any letter case, with no embedded IPv4 part.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its customer-visible symptom; de-duplicates by request id, not by batch; integer-only nanosecond arithmetic; bytes and cached bytes weighted like requests; the full set of cached statuses; IPv6 networks by parsed /64 prefix; a minimal, linear fix; a regression test per bug; sensible answers on sampling, late data and memory.

clarifications.q: Is a repeated line always in a different batch?
clarifications.a: Usually, because retries resend the batch under a new id. A line is a repeat if its ray was already counted, whatever the batch.

clarifications.q: Should distinct networks be scaled by the sample interval?
clarifications.a: No. Report the networks seen in the counted lines, unweighted. Estimating the unsampled count is a follow-up.

clarifications.q: Is ts_ns ever a float?
clarifications.a: No, it is always an integer. Keep it that way.

clarifications.q: Are 2001:db8::1 and 2001:db8:0:0::2 the same network?
clarifications.a: Yes. Both have the /64 prefix 2001:db8:0:0.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Compute an hour by hand for a line at the last nanosecond before an hour boundary, first with the code's arithmetic and then with integers only.
Read the de-duplication key and ask what a retried batch changes and what it keeps.
Write two IPv6 addresses for the same /64 in different forms and pass them to _network.
Check that every total that depends on sampling multiplies by the same weight.
followups: The network count is from sampled lines only. How would you estimate the number of distinct networks for a zone sampled at 1 in 100, and how confident could you be?
Retried batches can arrive hours later. How long must you remember ray ids, and how do you bound that memory across all zones?
A late batch arrives for an hour already shown to the customer. How do you update the rollup, and what does the dashboard show while it changes?
Customers want the same rollup per country and per status code. How do you avoid one pass per breakdown, and which totals can be added across breakdowns?

rules.ask: At what size does a float stop representing every nanosecond exactly, and how far from it is today's epoch in nanoseconds?
How long does your seen-set live, and what happens to a retry that arrives after you have forgotten the ray id?
Why group IPv6 clients by /64 rather than by full address, and what would grouping IPv4 by /24 change for the customer?
Which output columns can be scaled by the sample interval and which cannot, and why?
Can you merge your per-hour sketches into a per-day count, and what error would you quote to the customer?

templates.title: Logs delivery to customer destinations — batching, retries and proving completeness
templates.subtopic: push delivery to external sinks, batching, retries, completeness manifests

sections.scenario: Customers of an edge network can ask for their request logs, firewall events and other datasets to be pushed to a destination they own: an object-storage bucket, an HTTP endpoint or a log analytics service. Each customer configures a delivery job: which dataset, which fields, an optional filter and sample rate, and a destination. There are about {{jobs}} jobs, and together they carry about {{volume}}, produced at hundreds of locations worldwide. Jobs deliver files every {{batch_window}} or so. Destinations are outside your control: they throttle, reject credentials after a key rotation, or disappear for up to {{outage}}. Customers ask one question above all: did I get every log line?
sections.problem: Design the delivery pipeline from the moment a log line exists at an edge location to the moment a file lands at the customer's destination. Cover where lines are collected and buffered, how they are grouped into per-job batches, the file naming and content, the retry policy and back-off per destination, what happens to a destination that is down for {{outage}}, how one slow destination is kept from delaying other jobs, how a job's configuration change takes effect, and how you prove completeness to the customer: what they can check on their side and what you show them.
sections.constraints: Delivery is at least once; a retry can produce a duplicate file, so the customer must be able to tell. Lines from different jobs must never be mixed. The pipeline must not buffer unboundedly for a dead destination. Customers' credentials for destinations are secrets and never appear in logs or analytics. In this exercise's rule, a job may be disabled after a long run of failures and the customer notified (check current docs for real product behaviour).
sections.assumptions: All volumes, windows and limits are hypothetical. Each log line carries a unique request id and its event time. You may use common building blocks: a partitioned log, object storage for staging, a scheduler and a stream processor. Nothing here describes how any real edge network is operated.
sections.criteria: Collection decoupled from per-job delivery, with bounded per-job backlogs and isolation between jobs; deterministic file names and sequence numbers that make retries recognisable; a clear rule for event-time windows and late lines; per-window manifests or counts the customer can check; retry and back-off with a documented give-up point and notification; configuration changes applied at a recorded boundary; secrets kept out of logs; sampling visible in the output; a cost and sizing argument.

clarifications.q: Is the batch window by event time or by arrival time?
clarifications.a: You decide, and you must say what the customer can conclude from a file's time range.

clarifications.q: Can the customer filter fields and sample?
clarifications.a: Yes, per job. Sampling is part of the job's configuration and must be visible in what you deliver.

clarifications.q: How late can a line be?
clarifications.a: Most lines reach the pipeline within seconds; a location that loses connectivity can send lines up to an hour late.

clarifications.q: What does the customer see if their bucket is unreachable?
clarifications.a: Today, nothing until files reappear. Part of your design is what they should see.

clarifications.q: Is exactly once required?
clarifications.a: No. At least once with a way to detect duplicates is the contract.

hints: Separate collection (durable, independent of destinations) from delivery (per job, retryable). A dead destination should only make one job's backlog grow.
Give every file a deterministic name from the job, the time window and a sequence number, so a retried upload overwrites or is recognisably the same file.
A completeness claim needs a count. Publish, per window, how many lines the job should contain and which files carry them.
followups: A customer's destination is down for {{outage}}. Walk through what you keep, for how long, what you drop, and what the customer sees and can recover afterwards.
A customer says lines are missing for one hour. What evidence can you and they look at, and how do you tell a gap in delivery from a gap in traffic?
A customer changes a job's filter at 12:00:30. Which lines are delivered under which configuration, and how do they know?
One destination accepts uploads at a tenth of the rate you send. How do you protect the jobs that share capacity with it?
At {{volume}}, how do you size the batching layer, and what dominates the cost: compute, storage or egress?

rules.ask: The destination is outside your control and acknowledges after writing. Where exactly can a duplicate still appear, and how does the customer detect it?
How long do you keep retrying a destination that has been down for {{outage}}, and where are the lines kept meanwhile?
Who writes the manifest, when, and what does it say about lines that arrive an hour late for a window already delivered?
What is your partition key, and what happens to other jobs on that partition when one destination stalls?
When you finally give up on a batch, what do you tell the customer, and can they ask for it again?

templates.title: Measuring global key-value propagation — write-to-visible time, stale reads and a trustworthy dashboard
templates.subtopic: probes, clock skew, percentiles, customer-facing metrics

probe_rate: one write a minute per location
one write every 10 seconds per region

sections.scenario: An edge compute platform offers a global key-value store: a write is accepted in one place and becomes readable at every location eventually, and reads are served from the nearest location, possibly from a cache. In this exercise's rule, a write is expected to be visible everywhere within about {{target}} (check current docs for the real consistency model). There are {{locations}} locations and {{namespaces}} customer namespaces. Customers want to know how stale their reads can be, the product team wants to know when propagation is getting worse, and both want a dashboard they can trust.
sections.problem: Design how propagation is measured and reported. Cover what is measured (write-to-visible time per location, the share of reads that returned an older value, the age of what was read), how measurements are taken (synthetic probes, customer traffic, or both, at {{probe_rate}}), how you get correct durations when clocks at different locations disagree, how measurements are aggregated (per location, region, namespace and time window, with percentiles), how you handle probes that never see their write, and what the customer-facing dashboard shows and does not claim.
sections.constraints: Never read or log customers' values; metadata (keys hashed, sizes, versions, timestamps) only. Clocks at different locations may differ by tens of milliseconds and occasionally by seconds. Percentiles must be correct when combined across locations and windows. The measurement itself must not be a meaningful share of the store's load or cost.
sections.assumptions: The scale, target and probe rates are hypothetical. Each stored value carries a version or write timestamp from the location that accepted it. Locations can run small probe programs and report to a central pipeline. Nothing here describes how any real network or store is operated.
sections.criteria: A precise definition of propagation time and of a stale read; probes and customer-read signals combined with what each can prove; durations measured on one clock where possible and skew handled explicitly elsewhere; censored measurements kept rather than dropped; mergeable histograms or sketches for percentiles across locations and windows; no customer values read or logged; a dashboard that states its definition, coverage and uncertainty; measurement cost bounded; credible answers on clock jumps, regional regressions and customer complaints.

clarifications.q: Can I use customer reads, or only synthetic probes?
clarifications.a: Both are open to you. Customer reads tell you what customers saw; probes give a controlled, continuous signal. Say what each can and cannot prove.

clarifications.q: What is a stale read?
clarifications.a: A read that returned a version older than the newest version accepted at least {{target}} earlier. You may refine that definition, but state it.

clarifications.q: How good are the clocks?
clarifications.a: Synchronised, but not perfectly. Assume tens of milliseconds normally and occasional jumps of seconds.

clarifications.q: Who sees the dashboard?
clarifications.a: Customers see their own namespaces and global health. The product team sees everything, including per-location detail.

clarifications.q: Is a write that never arrives at a location possible?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, yes, rarely, until repaired. Your measurement must notice it.

hints: Measure a duration with one clock where you can: a probe that writes and then polls from the same location avoids skew for that leg. For cross-location timing, carry the write's timestamp and estimate the skew.
Percentiles do not average. Keep histograms or mergeable sketches per location and window, and merge them.
A probe that has not seen its write yet is not missing data. It is a censored measurement, and dropping it makes the numbers look better than they are.
followups: One location's clock jumps by 4 seconds for ten minutes. What does your dashboard show, and how do you detect and correct it?
The p99 write-to-visible time doubles in one region. How would you tell a propagation problem from a probe problem?
A customer says their reads were stale for 5 minutes yesterday, and your dashboard shows nothing. What can you check, without reading their values?
How would you show a customer the staleness of their own namespace when it gets only a few writes a day?
At {{namespaces}} namespaces, which aggregates do you keep per namespace, and which only globally?

rules.ask: The average write-to-visible time is 2 seconds. What does that say about the slowest location, and what would you show instead?
How do you combine p99 across 300 locations and 60 one-minute windows, and why is averaging the p99s wrong?
Which leg of your measurement depends on two clocks, and how big must the skew be before it changes what you report?
A probe gives up after 5 minutes without seeing its write. Does that become a 300-second sample, a missing sample, or something else, and why?
Customer reads tell you a version, not when it was written elsewhere. What extra metadata would you need, and can you get it without reading values?

templates.title: Zones and DNS records with history — who changed what, proxied or DNS-only, and the zone as of a date
templates.subtopic: configuration history, bitemporal as-of views, actor attribution

sections.scenario: Customers manage about {{zones}} zones (a domain and its DNS records) on a global network. A zone holds records of several types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT and others); in this exercise an address or CNAME record can be proxied, so resolvers receive the network's edge addresses and traffic flows through it, or DNS-only, so resolvers receive the record's own value. Records change about {{daily_changes}} times a day; {{api_share}} of changes come through the API (often from customers' automation, with an API token), the rest from the dashboard by a signed-in member of the account. Support engineers, customers and analytics teams all ask the same kinds of questions: who changed this record, what did the zone look like last Tuesday at 14:00, and how many zones moved a record from DNS-only to proxied this month. Changes must stay answerable for {{history_years}} years.
sections.problem: Design the data model for zones, records and their history. Cover: the zone and record entities with their keys (a record's identity across edits); how each change is captured (create, update, delete, proxied toggle, bulk import) with the actor (member or token, and through which interface) and the reason or request id; how to answer "the zone as of an instant" and "every change to this record" efficiently; how a change that writes the same value is treated; and the facts that answer "zones switching records between proxied and DNS-only per month" and "changes per zone by interface".
sections.constraints: History is append-only; a deleted record stays answerable. The as-of view of a zone must be exact to the second for the {{history_years}}-year window. Actor ids are stable even if the member leaves the account or the token is deleted. Record values can contain customer data (for example TXT verification strings), so analytics facts carry types, flags and counts, never values.
sections.assumptions: Zone counts, change rates, shares and retention are hypothetical. Proxied versus DNS-only behaviour, record types and TTL rules are this exercise's rules; check current docs. Several records can share a name and type (for example several A records for one name).
sections.criteria: Stable record identity across edits; an append-only change log with before and after images, actor (member or token id) and interface; versioned records with validity intervals for exact as-of queries; no-op writes recorded distinctly and excluded from change counts; bulk imports as one atomic change set; record values kept out of analytics facts; facts at stated grains for proxied toggles and changes by interface; retention for the stated years; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: If two records share a name and type, how do I tell them apart?
clarifications.a: Each record has an id assigned at creation; an update keeps the id, a delete-and-recreate gets a new one.

clarifications.q: Does a bulk import replace the whole zone?
clarifications.a: It can. In this exercise an import either adds records or replaces all records of the zone, in one request.

clarifications.q: Do we need to know who changed a record if they used an API token?
clarifications.a: Yes: the token id, the account member who created it, and the interface (API or dashboard). The token's secret is never stored.

clarifications.q: Is a change that writes the same value a change?
clarifications.a: Your choice. Automation often re-applies the whole configuration; say how you record it and how it shows in history and in counts.

clarifications.q: What does "as of" mean when a change is made in the dashboard but takes a moment to reach resolvers?
clarifications.a: Use the time the change was committed. Say whether you would also record when it was first served, and why.

hints: Separate the current state (one row per live record) from the change log (one row per change, with before and after images and the actor). The current state is a projection of the log.
For "as of", store each record version with a validity interval [valid_from, valid_to); then the zone at instant t is every version whose interval contains t.
The proxied flag is part of the record version; a toggle is a change like any other, and the monthly fact counts toggles from the log, not from snapshots.
followups: Write the query, against your model, for the zone as of a given instant. Which index or partitioning makes it fast for a zone with 5,000 records and {{history_years}} years of edits?
A customer's automation re-applies every record each hour. How does your model keep history readable, and how do the change counts avoid counting no-ops?
A bulk import replaced every record of a zone. Show what the change log holds, and what the as-of view shows one second before, during and after.
The member who made a change has left the account and the token used is deleted. What does a support engineer see for "who changed this", and what must never be shown?

At {{daily_changes}} changes a day, what grain do you keep in the warehouse for {{history_years}} years, and how do you compute "zones that switched a record to proxied this month" without scanning every version?

rules.ask: A record was changed three times on Tuesday. With the row updated in place, how do you answer what resolvers received at 14:00?
A record was proxied for forty minutes between two snapshots. Does your model show that it ever happened, and who did it?
Two edits to the same record arrive within the same second from two tokens. How do you order them, and what stops the intervals from overlapping?
Which of these columns may reach the analytics warehouse, and how do you answer "what changed" for support without copying values into facts?
The record is deleted and a new one with the same name and type is created a minute later. Is that the same record in your model, and what does history show?

incidents: A customer's automation re-applies every record of its zones every 10 minutes. With about {{api_share}} of changes coming from the API, no-op writes swamp the change log, and the one real edit support needs is buried under thousands of identical rows.

A replace-all import was implemented as delete-every-record followed by create-every-record in separate commits. For a few seconds the as-of view shows the zone with no address records, and a customer's audit report says their site had no DNS for that time.

Months later a support engineer asks who disabled proxying on a customer's apex record. The token that made the change was deleted, and the change log stored only the token's display name, which another token now uses.

templates.title: WAF rules as data — rule sets, versions, per-zone overrides, and which version matched a request
templates.subtopic: versioned configuration, override layering, event-to-version attribution

sections.scenario: About {{zones_with_rules}} zones use web application firewall rules. In this exercise there are two kinds: custom rules that a customer writes (an expression over request fields such as path, method or country, and an action such as block, challenge, log or skip), and managed rule sets that the provider publishes about {{managed_releases_per_month}} times a month, which a customer deploys to a zone and adjusts with overrides (turn a rule off, change its action, or change the sensitivity of a group). Rules can be deployed at account level (applied to every zone of the account) or zone level, and run in a defined order. Customers change rules about {{rule_changes_per_day}} times a day. Every request that a rule acts on produces a security event, kept for {{event_retention_days}} days. Customers ask "why was this request blocked, by exactly which rule and version?" and "what did my rules look like when it happened?".
sections.problem: Design the data model for rules and their history. Cover: custom rules and their versions (expression, action, order, enabled); managed rule sets, their releases and the rules each release contains; deployments of a rule set or rule list to an account or zone; overrides and how they layer (account, zone, rule set, group, rule); the effective configuration of a zone at an instant; and what a security event must carry so that it can be traced to the exact rule version and override that produced its action. Show the facts that answer "events by rule version and action per zone per day" and "how often an override changed a managed rule's action".
sections.constraints: A security event must be attributable to the rule version that matched, even after the rule is edited or deleted. Configuration history is append-only. A managed release is immutable once published. Expressions are customer configuration and can be shown to that customer, but security events carry ids and versions, not copies of expressions.
sections.assumptions: Counts, rates and retention are hypothetical. Rule kinds, actions, evaluation order and override layering are this exercise's rules; check current docs. A request can be matched by several rules; the event records the rule whose action was final, and in this exercise also lists rules that only logged.
sections.criteria: Rules, versions and managed releases immutable once published; deployments with scope and order over time; overrides as versioned rows with explicit precedence; an effective configuration per zone with a version id stamped on each event; events carrying ids and versions, not expressions; facts at stated grains for events by rule version and override effects; retention reconciled between events and configuration; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: If a customer edits a rule, is it the same rule?
clarifications.a: Yes, same rule id, new version. Deleting and recreating gives a new id.

clarifications.q: Which override wins when the account and the zone both override the same managed rule?
clarifications.a: In this exercise the most specific wins: rule over group over rule set, and zone over account. Say how your model makes that resolution reproducible.

clarifications.q: Can a managed release rename or remove a rule?
clarifications.a: It can remove one; rule ids are never reused. An override that points at a removed rule no longer applies, and the customer should be told.

clarifications.q: Does the event store the expression that matched?
clarifications.a: No. It stores ids and versions; the expression is looked up from the configuration history when someone asks.

clarifications.q: What about requests that no rule acted on?
clarifications.a: They produce no security event. Total request counts come from ordinary request analytics, not from this model.

hints: Model three layers apart: definitions (rules and their versions, managed releases), deployments (what is attached to which account or zone, in which order, from when), and overrides (versioned, with a scope). The effective configuration is derived from all three at an instant.
Give every effective configuration a version id (or hash) per zone, and stamp it on each security event; attribution then needs no time-range join.
Store overrides as rows keyed by scope and target, not as a JSON blob on the deployment, so "how often was this rule overridden" is a query.
followups: Write how you compute the effective action of one managed rule in one zone at an instant, given account and zone overrides. Where does that run: at event time, at deploy time, or at query time?
A customer edits a rule and reverts it two minutes later. Which version do events in those two minutes carry, and how does the customer see the difference?
A managed release removes a rule that 30,000 zones had overridden. What does your model record, and how do you show affected customers?
Events are kept {{event_retention_days}} days but configuration forever. What does a customer get when they ask about a request older than that?
With {{rule_changes_per_day}} changes a day and {{zones_with_rules}} zones, how large is the effective-configuration history, and would you materialise it or derive it on demand?

rules.ask: How would you answer "how many zones changed this managed rule's action to log last month" if overrides live inside one JSON document per deployment?
An event is stamped one millisecond after a deployment. How do you know which configuration it saw, given clocks and propagation, and would a configuration version id on the event remove the guess?
The rule was edited after the event. If you join the event to the current rule, what does the customer see as the reason it was blocked?
Where does the expression live, who may see it, and why not copy it onto each security event?
Two rules both match; one blocks and one skips. How does your model show which ran first and why the final action was what it was?

incidents: A managed release, one of about {{managed_releases_per_month}} a month, removes a rule that many zones had turned off with an override. The same detection now lives under a new rule id, and those zones start blocking requests their owners had deliberately allowed.

A customer asks why a checkout request was blocked 20 days ago. The event records the rule id but not its version, and the rule has been edited three times since; support shows the current expression, which would not have matched that request.

Security events by rule version show a version that was live for only 90 seconds receiving events for 10 minutes: attribution was done by joining event time to deployment time, while the configuration reached some locations later than others.

templates.title: Cache rules and their effect — order, TTL overrides, cache keys and which rule applied to each request
templates.subtopic: ordered rule evaluation, cache-key definitions, per-request rule attribution

sections.scenario: Customers control caching for their zones with an ordered list of up to {{rule_limit}} cache rules per zone. In this exercise a rule has a match expression (for example a hostname, a path prefix or a file extension) and settings: cache eligibility (eligible or bypass), an edge TTL override, a browser TTL override, and a cache key definition (which query-string parameters are included or ignored, and whether a header or cookie value is part of the key). Every matching rule applies in order and a later rule's setting wins where two rules set the same thing; without a rule, eligible content uses a default edge TTL of {{default_ttl}}. Zones serve about {{daily_requests}} requests a day; request analytics records each request's cache status (for example hit, miss, expired, revalidated, bypass) and, in this exercise, a {{log_sample}} sample of detailed request logs is available for analysis. Customers ask "which rule decided how this request was cached?" and "did my new rule raise my hit ratio, and did it serve anyone the wrong variant?".
sections.problem: Design the data model for cache rules and their effect. Cover: rules and rule-list versions (order matters); the settings each rule can set and how the effective settings for a request are resolved from all matching rules; how the cache key definition is represented so that two requests can be shown to share or not share a cache entry; what each request record must carry to attribute its outcome (rule-list version, the rules that matched, the rule that set each effective setting, the cache key fingerprint); and the facts that answer "hit ratio per zone and rule per hour", "requests whose TTL came from an override" and "distinct cache keys per URL path".
sections.constraints: A rule-list version is immutable once deployed; reordering is a new version. Effective settings must be reproducible from the stored definitions for any past request. Query strings and headers can contain personal data: logs and facts carry a fingerprint of the cache key and the names of the parts used, never raw values. Sampled data must be weighted to estimate totals.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, limits, sampling rate and the default TTL are hypothetical. Rule evaluation order, override precedence, cache statuses and cache-key options are this exercise's rules; check current docs. Origin cache headers are out of scope unless you choose to model them.
sections.criteria: Immutable rule-list versions with order; per-setting resolution with the rule that set each setting recorded; cache key definitions as data with a fingerprint, never raw values; request records carrying the rule-list version and matched rules; a stated hit-ratio definition (statuses in numerator and denominator); sampled facts weighted, with their uncertainty shown and reconciled to complete totals; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: If two matching rules set edge TTL, which wins?
clarifications.a: The later one in the list, in this exercise. A rule that sets only the cache key does not change the TTL set by an earlier rule.

clarifications.q: Do I get every request's details?
clarifications.a: Totals by cache status come for all requests from request analytics; detailed records come only for a {{log_sample}} sample, each with its sample weight.

clarifications.q: Is "revalidated" a hit?
clarifications.a: Say what you choose and why; it saves the origin a full response but still contacts it.

clarifications.q: Can I record the raw query string?
clarifications.a: No. Record which parameters were included in the key and a fingerprint of the resulting key.

clarifications.q: Does a change to rules invalidate the cache?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise. A changed cache key definition makes new requests look up new keys, so old entries are simply no longer found.

hints: Keep definitions (rule-list versions, rules, settings) apart from outcomes (request records). The link is the rule-list version plus, per request, the matched rule ids.
Resolve effective settings per setting, not per rule: for each setting, the last matching rule that sets it. Store which rule set each one, because "why" questions are per setting.
Represent the cache key definition as data (included parameters, ignored parameters, header or cookie parts) so a fingerprint can be recomputed and compared.
followups: Write the resolution of effective settings for one request given three matching rules, one setting eligibility and TTL, one setting only the cache key, and one setting bypass.
A customer moves a rule from position 9 to position 2. What does your model store, and how do you compare the hit ratio before and after fairly?
Detailed logs are a {{log_sample}} sample. How do you report hit ratio per rule for a rule that matched only a few thousand requests a day, and how sure can the customer be of it?
A cache key change starts ignoring a parameter used for asset versions. How would your facts reveal that one cache entry is now serving several different responses?
At {{daily_requests}} requests a day, which facts are built from complete counts and which from the sample, and how do you keep them consistent on one dashboard?

rules.ask: In this exercise every matching rule applies and later settings win. How does your resolution change, and which rule do you credit for the TTL?
The query string carries a session token for some customers. What does your request record keep, and how do you still show that two requests shared a cache key?
Is your hit ratio per request or per byte, and are revalidated and bypassed requests in the denominator? Say which and why.
How do you turn sampled rows into an estimate for a small rule, and what interval do you show the customer?
A request from last week was served under an older rule order. How do you reproduce its effective settings if you only have the current list?

incidents: A customer adds a rule near the top that ignores all query-string parameters for static files. The hit ratio jumps, but stylesheets versioned with a query parameter now serve the old file until the {{default_ttl}} default edge TTL lapses, and the dashboard showed only the improvement.

After a customer reorders their {{rule_limit}}-rule list through the API, the per-rule hit ratio report credits requests to rules by their current position, so last week's numbers move to different rules overnight.

Per-rule hit ratios built from the {{log_sample}} sample disagree with the zone total from complete request counts by several points for low-traffic zones, and a customer opens a ticket saying the analytics are wrong.

templates.title: Edge compute resources — scripts, versions, deployments, routes and bindings to storage
templates.subtopic: deployable artefacts, traffic splits, routing precedence, resource bindings and secrets

sections.scenario: Customers run about {{scripts}} edge compute scripts. In this exercise a customer uploads a script, which creates an immutable version (code plus its configuration); a deployment says which versions serve traffic, either one version at 100% or a gradual split between two (for example the new version at {{gradual_split}}). A script receives requests through routes (URL patterns on the customer's zones, such as a hostname and path with a wildcard) or a custom domain, and through scheduled triggers. A version declares up to {{max_bindings}} bindings: named handles to key-value namespaces, coordinated-state objects (each object class addressed by id), object storage buckets, other scripts, plain environment variables and secrets. There are about {{deploys_per_day}} deployments a day. Customers, support and the platform's own analytics ask: which version served this request, which storage did it touch, and what changed between Tuesday and Wednesday?
sections.problem: Design the data model for these resources and their history. Cover: scripts, versions and their bindings (each binding's name, type and target resource); deployments and splits over time; routes and custom domains, with how a request is matched to one script when patterns overlap; the storage resources themselves (namespaces, object classes, buckets) and their lifecycle; how a request or invocation record identifies the exact version and deployment that served it; and the facts that answer "requests and errors per version during a gradual deployment", "scripts bound to a given bucket on a date" and "routes that changed which script served a hostname".
sections.constraints: Versions are immutable. Secrets are stored only by name and binding type in anything outside the secret store: never their values, in configuration history, audit records or analytics. History is append-only and every change has an actor. Deleting a storage resource must not erase the record that scripts were bound to it.
sections.assumptions: Counts, rates, split percentages and binding limits are hypothetical. Version, deployment, route-precedence and binding semantics are this exercise's rules; check current docs. In this exercise the most specific matching route wins, and a hostname and path can be served by at most one script at a time.
sections.criteria: Immutable versions with binding rows; deployments with splits and validity intervals; versioned routes with explicit precedence; storage resources with stable ids and lifecycle; invocation records carrying script, version, deployment and route ids; secrets by name only, and plain variables treated as possibly sensitive; facts for per-version rollout comparison, binding history by resource and route changes; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a configuration change without new code a new version?
clarifications.a: Yes, in this exercise any change to code, bindings or variables creates a version.

clarifications.q: During a split, how is a request assigned?
clarifications.a: By a percentage of traffic; you do not control the assignment, but each invocation record carries the version that ran.

clarifications.q: Can two scripts' routes overlap?
clarifications.a: Patterns can overlap; for a given URL the most specific route wins. Your model must say which route won for a request.

clarifications.q: What happens to a binding when its namespace or bucket is deleted?
clarifications.a: The version still lists the binding; invocations using it fail. Your model should make that visible.

clarifications.q: Who may see binding targets?
clarifications.a: The account's members. Secret values are never visible to anyone after creation, including support.

hints: Treat version as the unit of configuration: a version row plus its binding rows (name, type, target resource id, or for a secret only its name). Deployments point at versions with percentages and a validity interval.
Give storage resources their own ids and lifecycle rows, so a binding references an id that survives a rename or deletion.
Routes are versioned too (pattern, zone, script, valid_from, valid_to). Matching a request to a route at an instant is a query over the routes valid then.
followups: A gradual deployment sends {{gradual_split}} of traffic to a new version. Write how you report error rates per version during the rollout, and what makes the comparison fair.
The new version binds a different key-value namespace under the same binding name. How does your model show which namespace each request's reads came from?
A customer deletes a bucket that three scripts were bound to. What does your model show the next day, and how do you answer "which scripts used it last month"?
Two routes overlap on a hostname; a more specific route is added for one path. How do you show, for one URL, which script served it before and after?
At {{deploys_per_day}} deployments a day and up to {{max_bindings}} bindings per version, how do you store binding history without copying every binding for every deployment?

rules.ask: Trace every place a secret's value could land in your design: upload, version record, audit log, analytics, support tools. Where is it stopped?
During a {{gradual_split}} split two versions serve at once. Which version does your invocation record name, and how?
Two versions use the same binding name for different namespaces. How does a query find the namespace a request actually used?
Two patterns match the same URL. Which wins in your model, and can you reproduce that for a request last month?
The resource is deleted. What happens to the bindings that pointed at it, and to the history that says they existed?

incidents: During a gradual deployment at {{gradual_split}}, the new version's binding pointed the same binding name at a preview key-value namespace. For two hours that share of requests read and wrote preview data, and the customer asks exactly which requests and keys were affected.

An audit export of version configuration for a customer included the values of plain environment variables, and one customer had stored an access key as a plain variable instead of a secret. The export reached a shared analytics table.

A customer adds a route that is more specific than an existing one on the same hostname. Requests for one path silently move to another script, and the analytics, which attribute requests to scripts by hostname, show no change.

templates.title: Rule changes and blocking — blocked share in the hour before and after each WAF deployment
templates.subtopic: event windows around changes, half-open intervals, LAG and LEAD boundaries, scope fan-out

sections.scenario: Customers deploy WAF rules to their zones and want to see what each deployment did to their traffic. The model has three tables: zones (each zone belongs to an account), waf_deployments (one row per deployment of a rule version, with status succeeded or failed) and requests (one row per request logged for a zone, with the final action: allow, block, challenge or log, and the rule_id that produced it, NULL for plain allows). {{scope_rule}} The report compares the zone's blocked share in the hour before a deployment with the hour after it.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns deployment_id, zone_id, requests_before, blocked_pct_before, requests_after, blocked_pct_after, change_pp: one row per succeeded deployment and zone it applies to, ordered by deployment_id, zone_id. A failed deployment never took effect: it gets no row and is ignored everywhere else. The before window is [deployed_at − 1 hour, deployed_at) and the after window is [deployed_at, deployed_at + 1 hour), both half-open. {{window_rule}} requests_* counts the zone's requests in the window; a request is blocked when its action is block (in this exercise challenges and logs are not blocks), whichever rule blocked it. blocked_pct_* is 100 × blocked ÷ requests rounded to 2 decimal places, or NULL when the window holds fewer than {{min_requests}} requests. change_pp is blocked_pct_after − blocked_pct_before, NULL when either is NULL. A deployment with no requests in its windows still gets its row, with 0 requests.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{zones}} zones, {{deployments}} deployments and {{requests}} requests; production has millions of zones and billions of requests a day.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, zones, rules and traffic. All timestamps are UTC. The reporting rules (what counts as blocked, the window lengths, the floor) are this exercise's rules, not a product's.
sections.criteria: Deployments as the driving rows, with a LEFT JOIN so quiet deployments keep their row; failed deployments ignored everywhere; half-open windows exactly as stated; at the harder levels, windows cut by the previous and next succeeded deployment affecting the zone, and account-level deployments fanned out to every zone of the account and used as neighbours; blocked defined as block only; the floor and NULL handling; numeric (not integer) division and rounding; deterministic ordering; can discuss pre-aggregation, attribution versus coincidence, sampling weights and propagation time.

clarifications.q: A request logged exactly at deployed_at: before or after?
clarifications.a: After. The before window ends just before deployed_at.

clarifications.q: And one logged exactly an hour after the deployment?
clarifications.a: Neither window of that deployment; the after window ends just before deployed_at + 1 hour.

clarifications.q: Should I count only blocks by the rule that was deployed?
clarifications.a: No. The report shows the zone's overall blocked share; rule_id on a request is informational here.

clarifications.q: Does a failed deployment shorten another deployment's windows?
clarifications.a: No. It never took effect, so it is ignored entirely.

clarifications.q: How should I round?
clarifications.a: PostgreSQL ROUND(numeric, 2) (half away from zero). Compute change_pp from the two rounded values.

hints: Start from the deployments, one row per (deployment, zone) it applies to, and give each its two window bounds. LAG and LEAD over the zone's succeeded deployments ordered by time give the neighbours.
LEFT JOIN the requests on zone and on the whole span [before_start, after_end), then count each side with COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) against deployed_at.
Apply the floor with CASE WHEN n >= {{min_requests}} THEN ROUND(100.0 * blocked / n, 2) END; integer division would truncate.
followups: At billions of requests a day, how would you serve this report per zone in seconds? What would you pre-aggregate, and at what time grain, given that windows start at arbitrary seconds?
The share went up after a deployment. What else could explain it, and how would you show a customer whether the deployed rule was the cause?
